All participants underwent nutritional screening through SGNA, 24-h dietary recall estimation, anthropometric measurements, evaluation of protein energy wasting (PEW), and quadriceps muscle ultrasonography. Results SGNA identified malnourishment in 85.3% of ESRD-HD children, while reduced/low muscle mass (LMM) by ultrasound was estimated in 73.6%, compared to PEW documentation in 70.6% of them. Total caloric intake discriminates LMM at a cutoff level of ≤34.022 kcal/kg/day with 93.75% sensitivity and 85.0% specificity and revealed a significant association with both PEW and LMM on regression analysis. Concerning concordance with muscle ultrasonography, SGNA had statistically good agreement, unlike anthropometric parameters. Conclusions Inadequate dietary intake, though highly prevalent, is still underestimated in CKD children with a negative impact on muscle mass. Also, SGNA, through combining objective anthropometry with nutrition-focused assessment, could represent a potential role for nutritional status evaluation. Impact Despite the absence of single gold standard assessment tool, PEW remains a prevalent, multifactorial nutritional comorbidity in CKD children that necessitates continuous nutritional monitoring. Quadriceps muscle ultrasound can detect changes in body composition associated with CKD, that cannot be determined just by objective anthropometry. SGNA, a simple malnutrition screening tool, showed a potential role in early prediction of both physical growth and body composition abnormalities. Dietary management for children with ESRD-HD should pay attention to total caloric, carbohydrate, and fat intakes, not just protein intake, for actual growth and body composition support.

title: A complementary proteomics and cardiac magnetic resonance approach to characterize right ventricular remodeling after tetralogy of Fallot repair
abstract: Abstract Background Patients with repaired tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) can develop right ventricular (RV) dilation and failure. We sought to utilize an untargeted serum proteomics approach to characterize the proteome signature associated with RV dilation in repaired TOF to improve the understanding of mechanistic drivers of RV remodeling. Methods Patients with repaired TOF undergoing cardiac magnetic resonance imaging were recruited. Groups were based on indexed RV end-diastolic volume (RVEDVi). Serum proteomics identified differentially abundant proteins ( p value < 0.05), and pathway enrichment identified functional pathways. Results Fourteen TOF adolescents (median age 16 years; IQR 15, 18) were divided into Group 1 ( n = 9; median RVEDVi 146 ml/m 2 ; IQR 139, 164) and Group 2 ( n = 5; median RVEDVi 114 ml/m 2 ; IQR 104, 130). Group 1 had a higher indexed RV stroke volume (85 ml/m 2 vs. 59 ml/m 2 , p = 0.023) with a similar RV ejection fraction. Group 1 had altered regulation of genes in multiple pathways, including glucose and fatty acid metabolism and antioxidant response. Conclusion Patients with repaired TOF and moderate-severe RV dilation have a distinct serum proteomic profile despite preserved ejection fraction, which may reflect alterations in fuel sources and oxidative stress. These hypothesis-generating findings are a first step in the integration of proteomics into clinical management. Impact An untargeted serum proteomics approach to identifying altered protein profiles associated with CMR-defined RV dilation is a novel approach to characterizing right ventricular remodeling after tetralogy of Fallot repair. RV dilation after repair of tetralogy of Fallot is associated with a specific proteomic profile suggesting adaptive and maladaptive remodeling. Identification of dysregulated proteins associated with RV remodeling provides insight into the mechanisms leading to ventricular failure after tetralogy of Fallot repair. With additional data from future larger studies, serum proteomics evaluation may assist in prognostication and clinical decision making in patients after tetralogy of Fallot repair.

title: Persistent postnatal alterations in microRNA expression in neonatal encephalopathy
abstract: Background Despite causing severe neurological morbidity, neonatal encephalopathy (NE) lacks reliable biochemical markers for early diagnosis and intervention. This study investigated if alterations in microRNA (miRNA) expression, previously identified in umbilical cord blood in NE, remain altered in postnatal whole blood samples. Methods Term infants with NE (and matched controls) born in Cork University Maternity Hospital (CUMH) between 2017 and 2020 were recruited. Whole blood was collected within the first 6 (T0), 24 (T24) and 48 (T48) hours after delivery via dried blood spot microsampling. Encephalopathy grade (mild, moderate, or severe) was determined based on modified Sarnat at 1 h. 19 candidate and three housekeeping miRNAs were analyzed in all infants via the 2 -ΔΔCt method. Results 66 neonates were included in the study; 53 with encephalopathy; (25 mild, 22 moderate and 6 severe), and 13 controls. 105 whole blood samples were taken across the three timepoints. Comparing NE (n = 28) with controls (n = 13) at T0 confirmed alteration of eight miRNAs, including newly identified miR-205-5p. Comparison of NE infants across the three timepoints found the persistent alteration of four miRNAs. Conclusion Persistent miRNA alterations are seen in NE 0-48 h postnatally and are detectable through minimally invasive microsampling. Impact Altered microRNA expression can be detected in the blood of neonates with neonatal encephalopathy when compared to healthy controls. These changes in expression are detectable in the postnatal period, up to 48 h after birth. Alterations can be detected through less invasive methods, showing promise that these microRNA profiles may serve as potential markers for the rapid detection of neonatal encephalopathy at the bedside. This follows on from previous research showing changes in microRNA expression in umbilical cord samples in encephalopathic infants, providing a longer window for potential detection spanning post-natally.

title: Impact of altered heme oxygenase-1 in caring for preterm neonates: navigating the unknown
abstract: Abstract Heme-oxygenase-1 (HO-1) is a key regulatory factor in organ development, organ function, cellular metabolism, heme processing, and bilirubin production. HO-1 homeostasis is crucial for healthy pregnancy and fetus. Dysregulation of HO-1 adversely affects placentation, yolk sac development, cardiovascular development, immune function, angiogenesis, microcirculation, alters the oxidoreductive balance, and is associated with adverse respiratory outcomes and necrotizing enterocolitis. The impact of HO-1 on neonatal neurodevelopment is unknown and is currently being investigated by our laboratory. In this review, we will discuss the morbidities associated with HO-1 dysregulation and importantly, we will navigate the unknown. We will highlight how infection or inflammation affect HO-1 homeostasis, its implications on neonatal morbidities at the limits of viability, summarize the relevant basic, translational, clinical and epidemiologic studies. We will conclude with proposing new approaches for the future, filling the gap between what is currently known and unknown. Impact What does this article add to the existing literature? HO-1 pathway is relevant to pregnancy, fetus, neonatal, and later life outcomes. Provides comprehensive organ systems-based evaluation of Heme-oxygenase-1 in pregnancy, fetus, extreme preterm, and periviable neonates. Highlights how environmental factors, including infection, inflammation resulting in systemic dysregulation of HO-1 affects major neonatal morbidities. Underscores that novel investigations to close the knowledge gap are forthcoming to transform the HO-1 field.

title: Isocaloric substitution of animal-based protein with plant-based protein and academic performance in Spanish adolescents: The EHDLA study
abstract: Background The source of dietary protein has been linked to cognitive outcomes; however, evidence on the association between isocaloric substitution of protein sources and academic performance in adolescents is limited. This study examined whether replacing animal-based protein with plant-based protein was associated with academic performance in adolescents. Methods This secondary analysis used data from the Eating Healthy and Daily Life Activities (EHDLA) study (n = 769; 55.5% girls; 12-17 years). Dietary intake was assessed using the 45-item food-frequency questionnaire. Academic performance was evaluated using grade point average and specific subjects (i.e., language, maths, and foreign language). Isocaloric substitution models were applied to estimate the association of replacing animal-based with plant-based protein, adjusting for relevant sociodemographic, lifestyle, and anthropometric factors. Robust linear regression was used. Results Replacing animal- with plant-based protein was consistently associated with higher academic performance across all outcomes (all p Conclusions Isocaloric substitution of animal-based protein with plant-based protein was associated with better academic performance in adolescents, highlighting the potential importance of protein source in dietary patterns related to educational outcomes. Impact Replacing animal-based protein with plant-based protein is associated with better overall and subject-specific academic performance in adolescents. This is the first study to apply an isocaloric substitution approach to examine the association between protein source (plant vs. animal) and academic performance in adolescents. Dietary patterns with a higher contribution of red and processed meat protein (relative to plant protein) were associated with less favorable academic outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of protein quality within dietary patterns and may inform nutrition-based strategies to support academic achievement during adolescence.

title: Stool biomarkers discriminate confirmed necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants
abstract: BACKGROUND: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in preterm infants. Early diagnosis remains challenging because clinical signs are nonspecific. We evaluated whether stool biomarkers could discriminate preterm infants with NEC from those without NEC. METHODS: We performed an ancillary analysis within the multicenter ClosNEC cohort of infants born before 32 weeks' gestation. Stool samples were collected at diagnosis in infants with confirmed NEC (Bell stage II or higher) and at comparable postnatal ages in preterm infants without NEC. Fecal calprotectin (fCal), human β-defensin-2, α1-antitrypsin (α1-AT), secretory immunoglobulin A (sIgA), cingulin (CGN), and eosinophil-derived neurotoxin were quantified using enzyme‑linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kits. Discriminatory performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis and logistic regression. RESULTS: The analysis included 130 preterm infants: 42 with confirmed NEC and 88 without NEC. Biomarker concentrations differed between groups for all markers except CGN. sIgA showed the best individual discrimination (AUC = 0.82), followed by fCal (AUC = 0.74) and α1-AT (AUC = 0.73). The four-biomarker model yielded an AUC = 0.83, whereas the six-biomarker complete-case model yielded an AUC = 0.86. CONCLUSION: Stool biomarkers discriminated infants with NEC from those without NEC. Our findings support prospective validation in infants evaluated for suspected NEC, including clinically relevant comparator groups. IMPACT: Stool biomarkers distinguished infants with confirmed NEC from infants without NEC in a multicenter cohort. Secretory IgA showed the strongest individual discrimination, with an AUC of 0.82. A six-biomarker complete-case model yielded an AUC of 0.86 in 108 infants. These biomarkers are potential candidates for further evaluation as noninvasive tools for NEC assessment. Validation is needed in infants with suspected NEC and competing neonatal diagnoses.

title: Claudin-3 in pediatric disorders of gut-brain interaction: promise and questions
abstract: Impact statement This commentary discusses serum claudin-3 (CLDN3) as a potential non-invasive marker of intestinal barrier dysfunction in adolescents with functional gastrointestinal disorders. Its association with systemic inflammatory markers raises questions about the relationship between barrier dysfunction and inflammation, while highlighting the need for prospective validation before clinical use.

title: Kata Kovacs: ECI biocommentary
abstract: I was born and raised in Győr, Hungary - a historic city along the Danube - where my early fascination with human biology and physiology set me on the path to Semmelweis University in Budapest. I earned my medical degree summa cum laude , laying the foundation for a career bridging bedside care and clinical research. I completed my PhD in Clinical Medicine while undergoing specialty training in Pediatrics. To broaden my methodological skills, I participated in the Harvard Medical School Foundations of Clinical Research program in 2022. Currently, I work as a postdoctoral clinical researcher and neonatology fellow at the Department of Neonatology, Pediatric Center, Semmelweis University. Alongside my medical and research career, Hungarian folk dancing has been a lifelong passion since childhood, and today I find balance as a mother of two little children.

title: AI-enhanced hemodynamic prediction of patent ductus arteriosus severity in premature infants
abstract: Background Hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus (HSPDA) requires timely assessment in premature very low birth weight (VLBW) infants. This study aimed to develop and validate an artificial intelligence (AI)-based surveillance system for predicting HSPDA and supporting real-time NICU decision-making. Methods We retrospectively analyzed electronic medical record data from VLBW infants with PDA admitted to the Samsung Medical Center NICU between 2013 and 2022. After excluding records with congenital heart disease or missing critical echocardiographic parameters, machine-learning models were trained on 85% of the dataset and tested on the remaining 15%. Results The best-performing model, Extra Trees, achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.829, with a sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value of 0.767, 0.766, 0.694, and 0.825, respectively. For transitional records shifting between hemodynamic states, the AUC, sensitivity, and specificity were 0.700, 0.722, and 0.606, respectively, based on the proposed transition-optimized threshold. Conclusion The AI-based Extra Trees model demonstrated a robust ability to predict the hemodynamic status of PDA in VLBW infants. Thus, it may help NICU clinicians optimize conservative management and improve clinical decision-making. Impact Our AI model achieves 0.829 AUC for predicting hemodynamically significant PDA in premature infants using routine NICU data without requiring echocardiography This study uniquely predicts PDA hemodynamic severity through multimodal clinical data integration, advancing beyond previous binary presence/absence classifications We introduce a transition-optimized threshold that detects dynamic hemodynamic changes, enabling precise monitoring during conservative management The model provides accessible real-time PDA assessment for resource-limited NICUs lacking immediate echocardiographic expertise, optimizing intervention timing and fluid management strategies Our validation across 1033 VLBW infants over 10 years demonstrates robust performance with only 12-h data requirements.

title: Persistent subclinical myocardial dysfunction among infants with Fetal growth restriction at one year of age
abstract: Abstract Background Fetal growth restriction (FGR) is associated with altered cardiac development and subclinical myocardial dysfunction; however, longitudinal data during infancy are limited. This study evaluated serial changes in cardiac structure and function in infants with FGR during the first year of life. Methods This prospective longitudinal study included 128 FGR neonates and 64 appropriate-for-gestational-age (AGA) neonates, of whom 39 early-onset FGR (EOFGR), 47 late-onset FGR (LOFGR), and 64 AGA neonates completed the 1-year follow-up. FGR was diagnosed antenatally using estimated fetal weight <10th percentile with abnormal Doppler findings and confirmed postnatally using Intergrowth-21 standards. Cardiac evaluation included conventional echocardiography, tissue Doppler imaging, and speckle-tracking echocardiography. Results At birth, FGR infants showed significantly lower anthropometric parameters and smaller cardiac dimensions compared with AGA controls. By 12 months, both FGR groups demonstrated catch-up growth with normalization of left ventricular dimensions and wall thickness. However, speckle-tracking analysis revealed persistent subclinical myocardial dysfunction. Global longitudinal strain and strain rate indices remained significantly impaired across follow-up. Right ventricular dysfunction was evident at 12 months, particularly in the EOFGR group. Conclusion Despite structural normalization and catch-up growth, infants with FGR exhibit persistent subclinical myocardial dysfunction during the first year of life. Impact Infants with fetal growth restriction exhibit reduced cardiac size and altered myocardial function at birth compared to AGA neonates. Both early- and late-onset FGR infants demonstrate significant catch-up growth and cardiac structural normalization by 12 months. Despite normalization of cardiac dimensions, speckle-tracking parameters (GLS and strain rates) remain impaired throughout infancy. Right ventricular dysfunction becomes evident by 12 months, particularly in early-onset FGR infants. Early myocardial impairment in FGR infants may represent a precursor to future cardiovascular risk, highlighting the need for longitudinal cardiac surveillance.

title: Evaporation dominates heat loss during skin barrier maturation in extremely preterm infants: a prospective longitudinal mixed-effects analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Extremely preterm infants exhibit immature skin barrier function, resulting in excessive water and heat loss. However, the temporal dynamics and mechanisms of heat loss remain unclear. Methods We conducted a prospective longitudinal study of infants born at 22–28 weeks of gestation ( n = 30). Transepidermal water loss (TEWL), insensible water loss from the skin (IWLs), and heat loss components were measured from birth to 28 days. Linear mixed-effects models were applied across four gestational age groups, adjusting for time-varying environmental conditions as management-related covariates. Results IWLs was significantly higher in lower gestational age groups and decreased nonlinearly over time. Maturation rates differed across groups. Evaporative heat loss consistently accounted for the majority of total heat loss across all gestational age groups. Environmental factors were associated with outcomes but reflected protocol-driven management rather than independent physiological determinants. Conclusion Skin barrier maturation follows a gestational age–dependent trajectory, and evaporative heat loss appears to be a major contributor to heat loss. Early evaporative control may play an important role in thermal management of extremely preterm infants. These findings suggest that both skin immaturity and environmental management factors contribute to thermal instability in this population, highlighting evaporation as a physiological pathway during early postnatal adaptation. Impact This study provides the first daily serial assessment of TEWL and IWLs in infants born at 22–28 weeks’ gestation. It enables the derivation of total heat loss on a day-by-day basis from direct physiological measurements. The findings further quantify the daily contribution of evaporative heat loss to total heat loss. These results offer new insights into heat loss dynamics and support targeted evaporative control in neonatal care.

title: Irrational antibiotic prescriptions in pediatric care across Africa: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Background Inappropriate antibiotic use, including deviations from guideline recommendations, incorrect dosages, and over-prescription, is a critical public health concern. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the prevalence and factors associated with inappropriate antibiotic use in pediatric populations across Africa. Method A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, and African Journals Online, following PRISMA guidelines and the PICOC framework. Study quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Meta-analysis was performed with STATA 17 using a random-effects model. Result From 3,085 records, 11 studies met inclusion. The pooled prevalence of inappropriate antibiotic use was 44%. Rates reached 75.1%, 73.9%, and 71.5% in some countries, while lower rates of 11% and 19.3% were reported elsewhere. Retrospective studies showed a pooled prevalence of 51.2% (I² = 99.5%), and prospective studies 35.4% (I² = 99%). Commonly prescribed antibiotics included cotrimoxazole, amoxicillin, and ceftriaxone. Inappropriate practices involved incorrect dosages (10.1%-19.5%) and durations (17.47-18.8%). Risk factors included younger age, three or more antibiotics (AOR: 2.8, 95% CI: 1.245-6.462, p = 0.013), and prolonged hospitalization. Conclusion Inappropriate pediatric antibiotic use in Africa is highly prevalent, driven by age, hospitalization, and polypharmacy, underscoring the need for targeted stewardship interventions. Impact This study is the first to bring together evidence across Africa showing that nearly half of antibiotics prescribed to children are used inappropriately. The findings call for stronger, targeted antibiotic stewardship efforts to improve prescribing practices and curb the growing threat of resistance in African healthcare settings.

title: Childhood tetralogy of Fallot repair outcomes in the modern era
abstract: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is a congenital cyanotic heart lesion that involves four structural components: ventricular septal defect (VSD), pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Long-term outcomes after repaired TOF (rTOF) are largely informed by historical cohorts, potentially limiting their relevance to patients treated in the modern era of advanced cardiac care. 1 The 2022 American Association for Thoracic Surgery (AATS) 2 guidelines recommend complete surgical correction between 3 and 6 months of age in asymptomatic infants. Palliative procedures are considered reasonable for high-risk infants. 2 The guidelines also endorse valve-sparing approaches, in addition to other recommendations 2 that were less standardized for TOF patients more than 40 years ago. Bitterman et al.’s article, 3 “Natural history of children after tetralogy of Fallot repair” published in a recent issue of Pediatric Research , addresses gaps in knowledge of rTOF outcomes in the current era. The authors utilize a single-center retrospective cohort study of TOF patients who were repaired between 2000 and 2015. In this commentary, 3 we evaluate the strengths and limitations of this study and identify areas for future research.

title: Beyond fatigue: optimising cardiac compression efficacy for the asphyxiated newborn
abstract: Chest compressions are among the rarest interventions performed during neonatal resuscitation, required in fewer than 0.1% of births. 1 Effective resuscitation, including chest compressions, is crucial in reducing morbidity and mortality in these infants. 2 , 3 Assessing compression quality and its relationship to meaningful clinical outcomes has proven challenging. Much of the available evidence continues to rely on simulation or animal models rather than clinical studies. Unlike adult resuscitation, where devices are available to provide consistent chest compressions with machine precision, 4 neonatal resuscitation relies solely on clinicians. Previous neonatal manikin studies have similarly demonstrated deterioration in compression performance with prolonged resuscitation. 5 For human performance to emulate a machine-like consistency, human factors such as fatigue need to be managed.

title: Decreasing uncertainty: using artificial intelligence to predict bacteremia and antibiotic need in sepsis in pediatric emergency patients
Neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants evaluated for but not treated with therapeutic hypothermia: a prospective cohort study
abstract: Background Therapeutic hypothermia (TH) is the standard of care for moderate to severe neonatal encephalopathy (NE). Although some centers consider TH for mild NE, neurodevelopmental outcomes of infants who do not meet eligibility criteria are incompletely defined. Methods Infants evaluated for TH based on perinatal risk factors, but who did not meet institutional eligibility criteria, were prospectively enrolled. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were assessed at 24 months. Bayley-4 scores Results Of 39 infants enrolled, 26 completed Bayley-4 assessments. Thirteen (50%) demonstrated sub-normative performance in at least one developmental domain; only one of them had an acute brain injury on MRI. Compared with infants with average-range performance, those with sub-normative performance had higher postnatal base deficits (10.1 vs 6 mmol/L, p 0.04), higher postnatal lactate levels (9.4 vs 4.9 mmol/L, p 0.05), and a trend toward less sleep-wake cycling on aEEG (45% vs 83%, p 0.06). Conclusions A substantial proportion of infants evaluated for but not treated with TH demonstrated sub-normative developmental performance at 2 years. Absence of acute MRI-detected injury does not preclude later developmental vulnerability. These findings support longitudinal follow-up of infants who are evaluated for TH but do not meet TH criteria. Impact Infants evaluated for but not treated with therapeutic hypothermia demonstrated a measurable risk of neurodevelopmental vulnerability at 2 years, with 50% demonstrating sub-normative performance (>1 SD below the normative mean) in at least one domain on the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development Fourth Edition. Early postnatal metabolic abnormalities in infants evaluated for therapeutic hypothermia showed a potential association with later developmental outcomes. There is a need for improved risk stratification and structured longitudinal follow-up for infants evaluated for but who do not meet cooling criteria.

title: Relationship between intra-thoracic pressure, lung volume and high-frequency jet ventilation in lungs predisposed to gas trapping: an animal study
abstract: Abstract High-frequency jet ventilation (HFJV) is used to manage severe respiratory failure in neonates, especially to manage gas trapping. To our knowledge, the role of HFJV rate on lung volume states and intra-tracheal and thoracic pressures has not been described. The aim of our study was to determine the impact of HFJV rate (HFJV rate ) on (1) total and regional end-expiratory lung volume (EELV) and (2) intra-thoracic pressure, specifically intra-tracheal pressure ( P trach ) and oesophageal pressure ( P oes ) in adult New Zealand white rabbits ( n = 5) prone to gas trapping. After stabilisation on HFJV (Bunnell LifePulse Ventilator; mean (SD) PEEP and HFJV PIP were 5.6 (1.3) cmH 2 O and 21 (2.6) cmH 2 O), HFJV rate between 150 and 900 bpm were randomly applied and regional EELV (electrical impedance tomography), P trach and P oes measured with gas exchange parameters. The non-gravity-dependent hemithorax demonstrated greater relative EELV with increasing HFJV rate , suggesting overdistension at higher rates. Δ P trach increased linearly from HFJV rate 150 to 900 bpm and conversely Δ P oes was more variable, decreased with increasing HFJV rate . There was a U-shaped relationship between HFJV rate and PaCO 2 with best CO 2 clearance occurring at HFJV rate 320–400 bpm. Impact In an animal model susceptible to gas trapping, high-frequency jet ventilation rate influenced volume state with increased carbon dioxide at low and high rates. This is the first study to define the mechanisms by which expiratory time during high-frequency jet ventilation alone can cause and relieve overdistension and atelectasis. Electrical impedance tomography was able to identify optimal lung volume, which may be useful in titrating the best high-frequency jet ventilation rate between 240 and 400 bpm for carbon dioxide clearance.

title: Using machine learning and physiological phenotyping to predict weight loss in adolescents
Signals, not verdicts: interpreting pediatric anaphylaxis reports from the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System
Small brainstem, big questions: linking neonatal brainstem size to neurodevelopmental outcomes after prematurity
Drugs associated with severe anaphylaxis in children and adolescents: a real-word FAERS pharmacovigilance study
abstract: Objective Based on the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS), drugs associated with an increased risk of severe anaphylaxis (SA) in children and adolescents were identified to provide a basis for safe drug use. Methods Adverse drug event (ADE) reports from the first quarter of 2004 to the fourth quarter of 2023 were retrieved from FAERS. The Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional ADR Reporting Ratio (PRR), Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) Combined Criteria Method, Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN), and Multiple Empirical Bayes Gamma-Poisson Shrinker (MGPS) methods were used in this study for mining drug signals. Results In total, 138 valid positive drug signals were obtained. Anti-infective drugs accounted for the highest cumulative number of ADE reports (845 cases). Of the top 30 drugs, ibuprofen accounted for 369 cases, and ceftriaxone was associated with the highest number of deaths. The drug instructions of human normal immunoglobulin (HNIg) and sevoflurane did not mention ADEs associated with SA. The prognosis for SA was poorer in younger children. Conclusion Monitoring of SA induced by antibiotics and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) should be continued in pediatric patients. The possibility of adverse reactions with HNIg and sevoflurane should be highlighted. Impact This study used data from the FAERS database to explore drugs associated with severe anaphylaxis (SA) in children and studied the prognosis of these reactions in children across different age groups as a reference for safer medication use in children. Among the positive drugs, the top three drugs with the highest number of adverse events were ibuprofen, infliximab, and omalizumab. In addition, there are two drugs (human normal immunoglobulin and sevoflurane) whose related adverse drug reactions for SA are not mentioned in the instructions.

title: Evaluating the AI-predictive potential of the PIC database for pediatric ICU mortality
abstract: Abstract Background Reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in healthcare depend on both data quality and model design. However, the predictive integrity of datasets is rarely assessed. Publicly available resources for critically ill children remain scarce. The Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database remains, to the best of current knowledge, the only open-access resource focused on pediatric critical care research. Methods This study evaluates the predictive potential of the PIC database. After applying strict cohort selection and data preprocessing, mortality risk was analyzed using statistical analysis through univariate Odds Ratio (OR) to measure associations, and machine learning (ML) models interpreted through SHAP values to assess feature importance and model behavior. Results ML experiments showed moderate but limited predictive performance for mortality. CatBoost performed best, with an AUC of 0.8521 (0.8414–0.8627) on the hold-out test set, but low sensitivity (42%) limited its ability to identify non-survivors. These findings suggest dataset-related constraints that reduce clinical reliability. Most relevant variables were minimum lactate, maximum lactate, mean respiratory rate, maximum hematocrit, and minimum urea. Conclusion Analysis showed that PIC lacks essential physiological data, highlighting the limits of current pediatric databases and the need for richer multicenter datasets to enable more robust, clinically applicable AI models. Impact Provides the first comprehensive evaluation of the PIC database, assessing its suitability for machine learning-based predictive modeling. Identifies key clinical variables and data gaps that influence the reliability of AI–based mortality prediction and model performance. Underscores the need for richer, multicenter pediatric ICU databases for research that incorporate essential physiological and neurological indicators. Demonstrates the value of combining statistical association and AI interpretability methods to assess the predictive integrity of clinical datasets.

title: Timing of onset defines distinct prognostic phenotypes in neonatal ards: a multicenter cohort study
abstract: Objectives Neonatal acute respiratory distress syndrome (NARDS) is a severe form of lung injury that poses a substantial threat to neonatal survival. This study aims to investigate potential variations in in-hospital mortality rates among NARDS cases based on the timing of disease onset. Methods This study utilized data from a multicenter retrospective cohort established by the Jiangsu Neonatal Respiratory Failure Collaborative Network. NARDS cases that received tracheal intubation followed by invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) were divided into the early-onset group (diagnosis within 72 hours after birth, n = 301) and the late-onset group (diagnosis after 72 hours of birth, n = 594) following the NARDS diagnosis. Results Late-onset was linked to lower mortality [hazard ratio (HR): 0.69, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.54-0.90]. After interaction adjustment, the HR derived from Cox regression analysis was 0.44 (95%CI: 0.28-0.70) with an E-value of 3.97. Interaction effect analysis identified an increased risk of death in late-onset NARDS complicated by pulmonary infection. Sensitivity analysis further confirmed the robustness of the results. Conclusions This study indicates that infants with late-onset NARDS who require intubation and IMV tend to have a more favorable prognosis, but newborns with concurrent pulmonary infections would have an increased mortality risk. Impact This is the first study to demonstrate that the timing of onset defines distinct prognostic phenotypes in neonatal acute respiratory distress syndrome (NARDS). We found that late-onset NARDS (developing >72 h after birth) is associated with significantly lower in-hospital mortality compared to early-onset NARDS. Crucially, this survival benefit is substantially attenuated in late-onset cases complicated by pulmonary infection, identifying a new, specific high-risk subgroup requiring heightened clinical vigilance. Our findings establish a simple yet powerful criterion for risk stratification and underscore the clinical heterogeneity within NARDS, paving the way for more tailored management strategies.

title: From oxygenation to omics: biomarkers as windows into pathophysiology and tools for prognostic and predictive enrichment in PARDS
abstract: In the article, “Unraveling Mortality Risk in Pediatric Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome: Key Biomarkers and Pathophysiological Insights”, Nimmankiatkul et al. impressively reviewed and contextualized many of the biomarkers with roles in mortality prognostication in PARDS. 1 Based on this work, what are some important takeaway messages and next steps to be considered related to the use of biomarkers in PARDS? Three important considerations include: 1) understanding the evolution of ARDS definitions and translational work over the last 50 years since ARDS was first described, 2) further exploration into the host responses to critical illness over time, and their roles in identifying biomarkers that can afford prognostic and predictive enrichment strategies for future trial design and bedside cares, and 3) reevaluating the relevance of mortality as a major outcome for ARDS related studies.

title: Pediatric nephrotic syndrome: a mini-review of genetic diagnostic methods
abstract: Abstract Idiopathic nephrotic syndrome (NS) is a prevalent glomerular disease that presents as either steroid sensitive (SSNS) or steroid resistant (SRNS), according to whether complete remission is achieved following corticosteroid treatment. SRNS is by definition only diagnosed after a failed 6-week steroid trial, exposing children to significant adverse effects. Moreover, SRNS confers an increased risk of progression to kidney failure, prompting early personalized treatment. Accordingly, clinically actionable tools that identify SRNS at disease onset are urgently needed to enable early risk stratification and guide precision therapy—distinguishing immune-mediated SRNS, which may respond to intensified immunosuppression, from monogenic forms that are typically multidrug-resistant and warrant avoidance of ineffective therapies and earlier implementation of targeted management strategies. Advances in genetics offer the potential to predict steroid resistance at presentation, enabling a paradigm shift toward personalized care. Established clinical diagnostics such as whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing are increasingly complemented by emerging research tools such as genome-wide association studies, epigenetic profiling, proteomics, microRNA analysis, and polygenic risk scores, although these remain largely investigational and not yet routinely implemented in clinical practice. This review highlights current and emerging genetic approaches for early NS stratification and their clinical applicability. Furthermore, we analyze key podocyte genes central to NS pathogenesis ( NPHS1 , NPHS2 and WT1 ). NPHS1 biallelic pathogenic variants are the main cause of congenital NS, particularly in Finnish populations, while NPHS2 mutations mostly underlie early SRNS onset. Monoallelic WT1 mutations cause both isolated and syndromic SRNS and necessitate oncologic surveillance. Accurate variant interpretation is essential for prognosis, therapeutic decision-making, and genetic counseling. Impact The current review highlights various genetic diagnostic modalities that can be used to detect and differentiate steroid resistant and steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome in children. The review analyzes key podocyte genes and their role in nephrotic syndrome disease characterization and importance of variant interpretation for prognosis and treatment planning. The review discusses the emerging role of non-invasive biomarkers and epigenetic mechanisms in distinguishing SRNS and SSNS and predicting disease progression.

title: From blood-expression signals to Kawasaki disease biomarkers: promise and limits of KLHL42 and SOS2
abstract: Impact Integrated blood-expression and genetic analyses nominate KLHL42 and SOS2 as candidate Kawasaki disease biomarkers; their opposing expression patterns were observed in a small patient sample. The two-gene score has not been validated as a locked test for febrile children, and the proposed butyrate pathway has not been directly demonstrated. Prospective studies in children with competing febrile diagnoses, paired metabolite measurements, and cell-specific experiments are needed to establish clinical value and elucidate the mechanism.

title: TLR8 in biliary atresia: linking innate immune signaling to fibrogenesis for therapeutic gain
abstract: Biliary atresia (BA) remains a ‘black box’ in pediatric hepatology, largely because effective pharmacological options to control the progression of inflammation and fibrogenesis that follow Kasai portoenterostomy (KPE) are lacking. 1 Innate immunity offers a compelling framework: perinatal viral exposure and dysregulated pattern-recognition signaling have been implicated in BA pathogenesis for decades, though with limited translational opportunities. Within this context, Toll-like receptor 8 (TLR8) has received comparatively limited attention. Long regarded as TLR7’s less-characterized counterpart, TLR8 has only recently gained a clearer structural and pharmacological definition, including selective chemical modulators and mechanistically supported pro-fibrotic role in dermal fibroblasts from patients with systemic sclerosis. 2

title: Beyond D-lactic acidosis: interpreting D-lactate after pediatric intestinal failure
abstract: Impact This commentary examines D-lactate beyond overt acidosis in children recovering from intestinal failure. Higher D-lactate after enteral autonomy suggests persistent metabolic differences but does not establish successful intestinal adaptation. Interpretation requires consideration of intestinal anatomy, nutrition, microbial fermentation, host metabolism, and renal handling. Preliminary pediatric reference values and urinary measurements require further validation before informing clinical decisions. Longitudinal studies should determine whether D-lactate predicts meaningful outcomes and improves care during intestinal rehabilitation.

title: Hypoxia-induced platelet activation and pulmonary platelets are increased in a murine model of neonatal chronic lung disease and pulmonary hypertension
abstract: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia-associated pulmonary hypertension (BPD-PH) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in preterm infants, yet available therapies lack mechanistic diversity and can be ineffective, highlighting an urgent need for novel therapeutic targets. Platelets are increasingly recognized as immune cells capable of driving pulmonary vascular inflammation, but their role in neonatal PH remains undefined. Neonatal mice were exposed to 12% hypoxia beginning at 12–24 h of life until postnatal day 8 (P8) or 15 (P15). Cardiopulmonary phenotype and markers of platelet activation were quantified using histology, flow cytometry, ELISA, and immunohistochemistry. Hypoxia produced a BPD-PH phenotype, including alveolar simplification, pulmonary vessel muscularization, elevated right ventricular systolic pressure, and right ventricular hypertrophy. Hypoxia disrupted the postnatal decline in pulmonary platelets and the platelet α-granule stored protein, platelet factor 4, resulting in increased pulmonary platelet accumulation at P15. Circulating platelets from hypoxic mice demonstrated increased activation, with higher P-selectin and activated αIIbβ3 expression at P8 and P15, enhanced agonist-induced P-selectin expression at P8, and increased leukocyte-platelet aggregation at P8. Postnatal hypoxia induces a robust, biologically meaningful platelet activation phenotype, supporting a previously unrecognized association between platelet activation and BPD-PH and identifying platelet activation pathways as potential therapeutic targets warranting further mechanistic investigation. Postnatal hypoxia drives persistent pulmonary platelet accumulation in a neonatal model of bronchopulmonary dysplasia-associated pulmonary hypertension. Hypoxic neonatal platelets exhibit increased P-selectin expression and αIIbβ3 activation, enhanced agonist responsiveness, and early leukocyte-platelet aggregation, indicating a shift toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype. These findings demonstrate that, despite developmental hyporesponsiveness, neonatal platelets are dynamically activated by hypoxia and may contribute to pulmonary vascular remodeling. This work identifies platelet activation pathways as potential circulating biomarkers and clinically relevant targets in neonatal pulmonary hypertension, expanding beyond current vasodilator-based therapies.

title: Azithromycin and childhood wheeze: Compelling biology, but does it translate into clinical benefit?
abstract: Wheezing illnesses are among the most common causes of respiratory morbidity and healthcare utilisation in childhood. Yet wheeze is a clinical symptom rather than a single disease process, arising from heterogeneous combinations of respiratory infection, airway inflammation, altered airway development and underlying susceptibility. This heterogeneity has complicated attempts to identify treatments that can be applied broadly across childhood wheezing disorders. Azithromycin is a particularly interesting example. Beyond its antimicrobial activity, it has well-recognised immunomodulatory effects on inflammatory cytokines, leukocyte recruitment and macrophage function. 1 Increasingly, however, clinical trial evidence challenges the assumption that demonstrating such biological effects necessarily predicts meaningful clinical benefit.

title: The need for SPeeD: can acute surfactant protein D administration reduce ventilator-induced inflammation?
abstract: Endogenous surfactant deficiency is a hallmark of preterm birth and the primary driver of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). 1 The development of exogenous surfactants in the 1980s led to a transformational increase in survival rates for infants born preterm. However, despite exogenous surfactant therapy being effective at reducing the acute severity of RDS, rates of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), the chronic lung disease consequence of preterm RDS, remain unchanged. 2 Endogenous surfactant is comprised primarily of phospholipids and surfactant proteins (A, B, C, D). 1 No commercially available animal-derived or synthetic formulas have successfully included all four proteins in their formulations, with animal-derived products containing only surface tension-reducing hydrophobic surfactant proteins B and C due to the purification process, and synthetic formulas including combinations of recombinant surfactant proteins A, B, C, or D, but never all four. 3 Animal-derived preparations remain the most commonly used surfactants as they are considered superior to synthetic formulations containing recombinants. Despite this, they lack the host defence immune-related functions that the hydrophilic surfactant proteins A and D perform. 4 Given that rates of BPD remain persistently high, it may be time to revisit the potential of recombinant surfactant proteins in exogenous surfactant therapy as a disease-modifying approach beyond mitigating acute respiratory distress.

title: Comparing MRI-based scoring systems for neuroprognostication in neonatal encephalopathy
abstract: Background Neonatal encephalopathy (NE) remains a significant cause of neurodevelopmental impairment. However, which MRI-based scoring system best predicts 36-month outcomes remains unclear. Methods A prospective cohort of 102 neonates ≥36 weeks gestation with NE underwent early postnatal brain MRI. Images were scored using five established systems: Barkovich, Weeke, Trivedi, Rutherford, and NICHD-NRN. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were evaluated at 36 months. Prognostic performance was analyzed using logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic curves. The best predictive model was determined using pairwise correlation to reduce highly correlated variables, and then backward selection to optimize the linear regression model. Results The Weeke total score showed the highest predictive accuracy for Bayley Scales of Infant Development motor outcomes (AUC 0.7647). The Weeke gray matter subscore was most predictive of Child Behavior Checklist internalizing problems (AUC 0.7735). No scoring system reliably predicted cognitive, language, or externalizing problems (AUC < 0.7). The optimal motor outcomes prediction model included 5 Weeke variables: basal ganglia, posterior limb of internal capsule, perirolandic cortex, cerebellar hemorrhage location, and basal ganglia lactate. Conclusions MRI-based scoring systems have limited prognostic value beyond motor outcomes after NE. The Weeke score offers the most reliable motor prediction, achievable using only five parameters. Impact Existing MRI scoring systems have limited prognostic value beyond motor outcomes after neonatal encephalopathy. The Weeke score offers the most reliable motor prediction. Only 5 Weeke scoring system variables are needed to optimize motor prediction. Deep gray matter injury is associated with internalizing behavioral outcomes. A simplified, user-friendly prognostic model can support accurate outcome prediction by a broader range of clinicians.

title: Air pollution and sudden unexpected death in infancy: a critical review of potential neurotoxic mechanisms
abstract: Sudden unexpected death in infancy (SUDI) is defined as the sudden death of an infant under one year of age. If a complete investigation (including a review of clinical history, an examination of the death scene and a full autopsy) fails to identify a specific cause, the death is classified as sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). 1 Some risk factors associated with SIDS are well known, such as infant sleeping position (the prone position being particularly risky), exposure to cigarette smoke, sleeping practices, sex (as the incidence is higher in boys), premature birth, and genetic predispositions. 2 , 3 One of the main hypotheses explaining SIDS is the so-called “triple risk model” of Filiano and Kinney. 4 According to this model, death results from the coincidence of three factors: 1) vulnerability (prematurity, intrauterine growth restriction, genetic abnormalities or prenatal smoke exposure); 2) a critical developmental period, with approximately 90% of deaths occurring in the first six months of life; and 3) an external stress factor, such as prone sleeping position, inadequate sleeping environment, exposure to tobacco smoke, etc. 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 Environmental exposure may play a particularly important role, both by increasing vulnerability and by acting as a trigger. Although most studies focus on SIDS, underlying biological mechanisms may extend beyond this category and also play a role in some deaths classified as explained. From this perspective, environmental exposures, including air pollution, could contribute to SUDI more broadly.

title: Enteric infection and childhood stunting: strengthening causal inference from heterogeneous evidence
abstract: Impact Laboratory detection of enteropathogens is associated with stunting in observational studies, but the pooled odds ratio does not estimate the effect of infection prevention or treatment on an individual child. Pathogen-domain and age-stratified estimates should not be read as equivalent causal effects; current data cannot reliably distinguish organisms, and environmental enteric dysfunction remains a hypothesized mediator, highlighting the need for prospective, longitudinal research to clarify causality. Prevention should integrate nutrition, infection control, and community-level environmental measures in the first 1000 days; empiric treatment of asymptomatic carriage is not supported, and prospective cohorts plus intervention trials are needed.

title: The emerging role of neutrophils in neonatal encephalopathy and hypoxic-ischemic brain injury: across human and animal neonates
abstract: Abstract Neutrophils, traditionally viewed as first responders to microbial invasion, also play a pivotal role in sterile inflammation associated with tissue injury or stress in the absence of pathogens. In this context, they are recruited by danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) released from damaged or dying cells, rather than by microbial signals. Once at the site of injury, neutrophils clear debris, release proteases and reactive oxygen species contributing to tissue damage, and shape the inflammatory environment through cytokine and chemokine secretion. However, because their antimicrobial arsenal is nonspecific, their activity in sterile settings can be a double-edged sword: essential for initiating repair but also capable of exacerbating tissue injury if not properly regulated. Neutrophils have been implicated in many diseases of neonates, particularly neonatal encephalopathy (NE). Recently, this has been demonstrated using different hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) animal models. Harnessing the roles of neutrophils, both good and bad, can potentially influence future clinical therapies. This review summarizes the current knowledge about the role of neutrophils following perinatal hypoxic-ischemic brain injuries. Impact This study elucidates the association between neutrophil activity and neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, thereby reinforcing emerging evidence from animal models and elucidating the underlying mechanisms of this prevalent neonatal condition. Neutrophils play a pivotal role in sterile inflammation, underscoring their dual function in both tissue repair and damage. This duality reshapes the understanding of injury, extending beyond the traditional focus on infection. Neutrophils have been recognized as potential therapeutic targets, and the modulation of their responses may achieve a balance between protection and injury. This approach could pave the way for novel, mechanism-based treatments for perinatal brain injury.

title: NICU escape rooms: an innovative, gamified approach to team-based interpersonal and communication skills education
abstract: Escape rooms have been studied in other specialties for the current generation of learners, but not in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). Gamification with escape rooms may address team-based interpersonal and communication skills education. Assess the impact of implementing a NICU escape room and its role in team-based interpersonal and communication skills education. Participants solved a series of puzzles using core neonatology knowledge to reveal a final clue. Ratings were evaluated using Likert scale-based post-activity and end-of-rotation surveys. Participation in the NICU escape room addressed team-based interpersonal and communication skills education compared to nonparticipants (mean 3.35 vs. 2.72, p = 0.03). Residents rated the escape room activity significantly higher than morning didactics, noon lectures, and teaching during rounds. There were no differences in the overall NICU education rating or degree of engagement between participants and nonparticipants. On the post-activity survey, mean ratings of the escape room exceeded 4 out of 5 for enhancing the educational experience, engagement, confidence, relevance, and use of interpersonal and communication skills in a supportive environment. NICU escape rooms are a modality for team-based communication and interpersonal skills education, are preferred over other teaching methods, and foster a positive learning experience. Escape rooms are an innovative way to address the gap in education regarding team-based interpersonal and communication skill development, which is of particular importance for trainees in a high-acuity setting. Escape rooms are an enjoyable, engaging educational activity that are preferred over other didactic methods.

title: Distribution of applied forces during face mask ventilation: a preterm neonatal manikin study
abstract: Background Resuscitators may apply different forces to optimize the mask seal during neonatal resuscitation. We investigated the distribution of applied forces across the face of a preterm neonatal manikin during positive pressure ventilation. Design This sub-study involved 30 neonatologists and pediatric/anesthesiology residents participating in a scenario of a preterm infant requiring face mask ventilation. The outcome was the force applied on the manikin face by the operator using a soft-cushion anatomical mask. Force was recorded by sensors positioned on the nose, right chin, central chin and left chin. Force-related indicators included maximum force, average peak force and standard deviation of applied forces. Results The sensors recorded higher median applied forces on the nose than on the right chin (maximum force: median difference [MD] 0.9 N, 99%CI 0.2 to 1.3; average peak force: MD 0.9 N, 99%CI 0.1 to 1.1). The sensors also recorded higher values of top 10th percentile of applied forces (maximum force, average peak force and standard deviation of applied forces) on the nose, central chin and left chin compared to the right chin. Conclusions The participants applied uneven forces across key points of the manikin face during face mask ventilation. Providing trainees with real-time feedback on applied forces may improve the acquisition of PPV skills. Impact In a preterm neonatal manikin model, health care providers exerted uneven force on different key points of the manikin face during face mask ventilation. The operator may be prone to apply more force on the hand-holding side. Offering real-time feedback on applied forces to trainees may improve the attainment of PPV skills.

title: Puberty timing and early adulthood plasma proteome and non-lipid metabolome: a twin study of genetic and environmental contributions
abstract: Abstract Introduction Pubertal timing influences metabolic disease risk, but its links to the plasma proteome and non-lipid metabolome remain unclear. We investigated associations of pubertal development with these profiles in early adulthood and examined genetic and environmental contributions. Data and methods Finnish twins (630, 57% female) reported pubertal development using the Pubertal Development Scale (PDS) at ages 11.5 and 14, and retrospectively via pubertal age (PA) at ~17.5 years. Plasma proteomics and metabolomics were measured at ~22 years. PDS and PA were tested against proteome and non-lipid metabolome molecules using linear mixed-effects models. Significant associations were decomposed into genetic and environmental components using structural equation modeling. Results Three plasma proteins (desmoglein-2, CD14, complement C6) and one metabolite (histidine) were associated with PDS at age 14. Desmoglein-2 ( r A = –0.08) and CD14 ( r A = –0.13) showed genetic but no significant environmental correlations. The C6 association reflected nonshared environmental factors ( r E = 0.31), with a non-significant genetic correlation. Histidine showed no clear genetic or environmental contributions. Conclusion Pubertal development at age 14 influences plasma molecules in early adulthood. Protein associations reflect both genetic and environmental contributions, with weak, suggestive genetic correlations. Puberty may thus be a critical period for long-term metabolic programming. Impact Pubertal timing at age 14 is associated with specific plasma proteins and metabolites in early adulthood, indicating early-life molecular signatures of metabolic health. Genetic factors may suggestively contribute to some associations (desmoglein-2, CD14), while environmental factors influence others (complement component C6), highlighting targets for personalized risk assessment. These findings suggest that puberty is a critical window for identifying individuals at risk of future metabolic or cardiovascular disorders, offering opportunities for early prevention and intervention strategies.

title: Refocusing preterm infant nutrition and growth research: will it lead to answers?
abstract: Impact statement Determining preterm infant nutrition and growth needs is complex; however, a standardised reporting framework will provide a foundation for identifying clear, actionable answers.

title: Navigating technical challenges in the care of infants born at the limits of viability
abstract: Abstract The resuscitation, intensive care and survival of peri-viable extremely premature infants (PVEPT) have been increasing in recent years. The initial care of these infants requires precision when performing a number of procedures after delivery. The multi-disciplinary team within the neonatal intensive care unit requires significant training with graduated autonomy to successfully perform procedures in this population. Preparation, performance and complications of endotracheal intubation, umbilical catheterization, percutaneously inserted central catheter placement, and orogastric tube placement in PVEPTs are reviewed. Experiential approaches are provided to bolster the discussion of these procedures when literature is limited. A review of PVEPT skin physiology is presented, and techniques to secure lines and tubes to minimize skin trauma within environments that do and do not utilize humidity are discussed. Impact The care of peri-viable extremely premature infants requires many precise technical skills from a multidisciplinary team immediately following delivery. Careful preparation, supervised technique, and an understanding of common pitfalls are paramount to procedural success in this population. Careful attention must be paid to the fragile neonatal skin to avoid pain and injury in this patient population.
